[[RunningHead]]

Child psychotherapy with looked after and adopted children: a UK national survey of the profession

Fiona Robinson , Patrick Luyten and Nick Midgley

Nick Midgley

London
UK
Department of Clinical, Educational and Health Psychology

Nick Midgley  

child psychotherapy, complexity, looked after children, adopted children, survey

Relatively little empirical data is available about the range of work undertaken by child psychotherapists in the UK; however, previous surveys have shown high levels of complexity amongst children referred to child psychotherapists and an increasing proportion of work with children in foster or adoptive placements. Aims: We sought to examine child psychotherapists’ working practices with looked after and adopted children (LAAC), including the types of activities undertaken and their views on this work. Method: An online survey was designed to elicit this information from the members of the Association of Child Psychotherapists (ACP), the regulatory body for child psychotherapists in the UK. The survey included a number of categorical and open-ended questions, which were analysed quantitatively and qualitatively. Findings: 215 responses were received (24.5% of the eligible ACP membership). The vast majority of the sample were working with LAAC in some context (87.9%). Respondents were conducting a range of work: the most frequently conducted activities were assessment (83.7%), direct psychotherapy (82.3%), work with foster carers and adoptive parents (80.9%) and consultation with the professional network (76.7%). Thematic analysis of qualitative data suggested the complexity of problems amongst the children attending psychotherapy, as well as the perceived need for long-term work with these children. Many respondents placed emphasis on the importance of working with the professional network around the child, including foster carers and adoptive parents, despite feeling that this was often an under-resourced area of child and adolescent mental health services. The implications of the survey for practice and future research are discussed.

Hillel Mirvis

Hillel Mirvis

Edgware
UK

Hillel Mirvis   *Email: hillelmirvis@hotmail.com
psychosis, adolescence, therapeutic alliance, transference, narcissism, disintegration

This paper discusses the challenges of struggling to build and maintain a therapeutic alliance with a psychotic adolescent boy who did not share an allied perception of reality with his therapist, and who insisted that his therapist did not exist. The paper poses the question of whether, under such circumstances, it is ever appropriate or tolerable to make transference interpretations. Drawing on detailed clinical material, the author attempts to make sense of how it was possible to make some contact with his patient, given these technical difficulties.

Research digest: adolescence

Introduction

By the time this issue of the Journal of Child Psychotherapy is published, readers are likely to have read in full the first article in our Digest, namely the results of the IMPACT trial reported in The Lancet in November 2016. However, as this trial, and the publication of its results, form a major milestone in the history of research in the outcomes of child psychotherapy, we make no apology for taking it as the starting point for this Digest. Any readers who have not yet read it should note that the article is Open Access and hence freely available.

The results have caused lively debate in psychotherapy research circles. The study has yielded a volume of data that has also spawned many other studies throwing light on different aspects of adolescent depression. Many of these other ‘spin-off’ studies are listed here. It is hoped that the wealth and richness of the data collected will continue to form the basis of further research in this field for years to come.

Many of the articles derived from the IMPACT data are qualitative and form part of the IMPACT-ME (My Experience) research arm led by Nick Midgley. Of note is the study by Stapley et al. on parents’ experience of their children’s depression, a little researched perspective yielding some surprising themes. Further, two studies by Midgley et al. take unusual and intriguing approaches, viz. young people’s experience of taking part in a randomized controlled trial, and young people’s ideas about why they have got depression. These are also well worth reading. There is also, naturally enough, a study about young people’s experience of depression, and a helpful methodological paper about the use of framework analysis as a qualitative research method (Parkinson et al.).

The second half of this Digest presents abstracts of studies unrelated to IMPACT, that throw light on various aspects of adolescent depression. Taylor et al. report on depression in young people with Chronic Fatigue Syndrome; and two studies address the potential relationship between parental depression and mental ill health, and that of their offspring (Kilford et al., Sweeney and MacBeth). Finally, given that depression in adolescence is so prevalent as to be taken as near normal in popular understanding, a report on a programme intended to improve GP detection and care of adolescent depression was considered germane (Kramer et al.).

[[RunningHead]]

The non-linear mind: psychoanalysis of complexity in psychic life

Margaret Lush

Margaret Lush

London
UK
Gloucester House

Margaret Lush   *Email: margaret_lush@yahoo.co.uk

Can we develop our understanding of the mind through the application of new approaches to the study of complex systems? What are the implications for clinical practice and research when we embrace the non-linearity of the mind more fully? These are the questions addressed in this thought-provoking book edited by psychoanalyst James Rose and child psychotherapist Graham Shulman.

137

In the Introduction Rose explains that the book is ‘titled The Non-Linear Mind because of the daily observation that the mind is complex and complex systems are essentially non-linear. What this means is that they cannot be adequately modelled mathematically using linear equations’ (p. xi). Psychoanalytic thought and practice, particularly in the Kleinian and post-Kleinian tradition, with its emphasis on the ubiquity of unconscious phantasy, links naturally with ideas from chaos theory and works implicitly with the idea of the mind as a non-linear system. In Shulman’s chapter ‘Some research implications’ he argues that Klein anticipated some of the applications of chaos theory and the significance of its central concepts in the following extract:

The primal processes of introjection and projection lead to constant changes in the ego’s relation to its objects, with fluctuations between internal and external, good and bad ones, according to the infant’s phantasies and emotions as well as under the impact of his actual experiences. The complexity of these fluctuations engendered by the perpetual activity of the two instincts underlies the development of the ego in relation to the external world as well as the building up of the internal world.

(Klein, 1958: 239)

Shulman notes that Klein captures a fundamental characteristic of mental life and experience as it is lived and evolves over time in terms of its ‘constant changes’, ‘fluctuations’, ‘perpetual activity’, and ‘complexity’ (p. 159).

A central concept in the study of non-linear complex dynamic systems referred to repeatedly by contributors is the strange attractor and this is the focus of Rose’s first chapter. He explains this highly complex concept, describing it as ‘a pattern of cyclical dynamic motion towards which such a [complex non-linear] system tends when responding to external stimuli, which disturb its internally determined processes in some way’ (p. 7). He discusses the idea of iteration (meaning in psychoanalysis broadly that the product of each psychoanalytic session must feed forward in some way into the next one) and outlines the argument he develops through linking these two ideas. ‘In essence, my argument is that the possibility of the observation and identification of strange attractors in psychic reality arises out of the continued iteration of the encounter between an analysand and his psychoanalyst’ (p. 10). This is then further developed into what Rose calls ‘the psychoanalytic iterating learning system’ (p. 102).

An independent mind: collected papers of Juliet Hopkins

Rajni Sharma

Rajni Sharma

Manchester
UK

Rajni Sharma   *Email: rajnisharma@nhs.net

This publication coincided with Juliet Hopkins’ 80th birthday in 2015 and is a collection of 12 papers gathered together into four sections: work with trauma; attachment theory; infant–parent psychotherapy; integrating and exploring Winnicott. The opportunity to read this book leads me to recommend it heartily as more than a sum of its parts, although I imagine that clinicians will dip in and out of it as needed. With a clear structure, it is an accessible collection that showcases Hopkins’ friendly intelligence and innovative insights analogous to the clinical companionship of an intuitive and encouraging supervisor. The evocative case studies readily connect with the day-to-day clinical encounters of child and adolescent psychotherapists and highlight the valuable learning that is offered by practice-based evidence. Hopkins’ clinical intuition, deep interest in her patients coupled with a facility with words opens up complex insights and extension of ideas succinctly, clearly and usefully. For example in one of Hopkins’ much cited papers, ‘Solving the mystery of monsters’ (1986), she discusses the centrality of containment in the recovery from trauma:

Many traumatised children entering psychotherapy are unready and unable to confront their past. They may benefit from spending long periods in which they communicate their inchoate and unprocessed experience through compulsive repetition in the here-and-now. It is the therapist’s capacity to tolerate, contain and process these negative experiences without joining the dance of rejection, retaliation, humiliation and helplessness that enables children to move beyond the need for re-enactment and to discover that relationships with adults are less frightening than they had believed. Perhaps Freud (1909) was right to suppose that ghosts of the past can never fully rest until they have been understood, but meanwhile the therapist’s capacity for containment can reduce the pressure to repeat the past and so allow new relationships to develop. (p. 15)

This volume makes a timely contribution to understanding the role of psychoanalysis, psychotherapy and psychoanalytic thinking in the NHS today. Author biographies

Louise Allnutt is a senior child and adolescent psychotherapist at the Tavistock Centre. She works in the newly formed Returning Families Unit. Until recently Louise was the lead child psychotherapist within a specialist CAMHS for children with developmental difficulties and disabilities. She has also taught on many aspects of the clinical training including theory, supervision and leading the autism workshop and has research interests in the area of early intervention with children at risk of autism and other social communication disorders.

Lida Anagnostaki is a psychologist and child and adolescent psychotherapist working in private practice in Athens, Greece. She also works as a research and teaching associate at the University of Athens. She is a full member of the Hellenic Association of Child and Adolescent Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy.

Robert Fleming is originally from Scotland, and became a social worker in South London before working in a child guidance clinic in America. He returned to the UK and trained as a child and adolescent psychotherapist at the Tavistock and later as an adult psychotherapist at the British Association of Psychotherapists (now BPF). Throughout his professional life he has had an interest in the substitute care of children unable to live with their birth parents. He completed his doctoral research in this area. Robert is currently a consultant child and adolescent psychotherapist with South London and Maudsley NHS Trust.

Lorna French is an assistant research psychologist in the Children, Young Adults and Families directorate at the Tavistock and Portman NHS Foundation Trust.

Marianne Haugvik trained as a clinical psychologist at the University of Oslo, Norway. She is a specialist in child and adolescent psychology and holds the position of Chief Psychologist at an outpatient clinic for children and adolescents in Oslo. Her main interests are developmental psychology and intersubjectively oriented time-limited psychotherapy, a method that she has participated in developing. She was the project manager of a research project related to this therapy method and is the author of a number of articles on this modality.

Discussing the therapeutic setting in child and adolescent psychoanalytic psychotherapy

Lida Anagnostaki , Alexandra Zaharia and Mata Matsouka

Mata Matsouka

Athens
Greece

Mata Matsouka  

therapeutic setting, active matrix, casing, modifications, ruptures in the setting

The aim of this paper is to contribute to a debate on the particular characteristics of the therapeutic setting in child and adolescent psychoanalytic psychotherapy and its differences from the setting in adult therapy. In our opinion, there is a fundamental difference between these two, as in child and adolescent psychotherapy two distinct aspects co-exist and in some areas, overlap. In this paper, we attempt to delineate these two aspects, following Green’s division of the analytical setting into the active matrix and the casing. We propose that in child and adolescent psychotherapy the therapeutic contract, the active matrix, concerning the necessary conditions for making a therapy psychoanalytic – namely, the therapist’s free-floating attention and the patient’s free associations – is agreed between the therapist and the child/adolescent. We argue that in contrast, the contract regarding the casing – the timings of sessions, the fees and so on – is agreed primarily with the parents or carers of the child/adolescent. Ruptures and possible modifications in both the matrix and the casing of the setting are discussed through the presentation of clinical material.

A place within the heart: finding a home with parental objects

Simon Cregeen

Simon Cregeen

Salford
UK

Simon Cregeen   *Email: simon.cregeen@cmft.nhs.uk
adoption, adoptive couples, psychic home, parental objects, projective identification, looked after children

For adopted and Looked After children with compromised early experiences, there can be troubling phantasies and anxieties associated with parental objects. These internal object relations can seriously restrict the development of secure intimate relationships with new parental figures. Adoptive parents and foster carers bear the brunt of the associated difficulties. Clinical work with the child, parents/carers, family, or network, may help processes of containment, differentiation, working through, mourning, and integration. This paper is based on thinking derived from clinical work with children who are adopted or Looked After, and with adoptive parental couples, carers, and networks. The primary focus is on how the child needs to find a ‘psychic home’ in the minds of others for their damaged internal parental objects, and the emotional capacities required in adoptive parents to provide this. I describe some of the complexities for adoptive parents and others in providing what is needed to enable the child to experience their internal parental objects in a fuller way. This process can allow the child to introject, identify with, and re-imagine their internal parental objects, and through this develop a more realistic relationship to their adoptive parents and to their birth parents. It promotes trust, freedom, and emotional depth in the relationship with parental figures.

The Herts and minds study: evaluating the effectiveness of mentalization-based treatment (MBT) as an intervention for children in foster care with emotional and/or behavioural problems: a phase II, feasibility, randomised controlled trial

Nick Midgley, Sarah Jane Besser, Helen Dye, Pasco Fearon, Tim Gale, Kiri Jefferies-Sewell, Karen Irvine, Joyce Robinson, Solange Wyatt, David Wellsted and Sally Wood

Pilot and Feasibility Studies, BioMed Central, 2017, Volume 3 (12), DOI: 10.1186/s40814-017-0127-x.

Background: A significant proportion of children in the social care system in England present with mental health problems, with the majority experiencing some form of emotional and behavioural difficulties. The most effective treatments for these children are currently unknown, partly due to a lack of robust, controlled studies. Researchers have identified a number of obstacles to conducting well-designed research with this population, making the need to test the feasibility of a randomised controlled trial especially important. Methods/design: This protocol outlines a two-arm, randomised control feasibility trial to explore the acceptability and credibility of mentalization-based treatment (MBT) as a treatment for reducing emotional and behavioural difficulties in looked after children and to test the possibility of addressing a number of methodological challenges to conducting high-quality research with this population. MBT is a relatively new intervention which, in the adaptation of the model tested here, includes many of the features of therapy identified in NICE guidelines as necessary to support children in care. The two arms are MBT and usual clinical care (UCC). The study will take place in Hertfordshire Partnership University NHS Foundation Trust with follow-up at 12 and 24 weeks. Discussion: This study will aim to ascertain whether it is worthwhile and feasible to progress to testing the intervention in a full-scale definitive randomised controlled trial (RCT). This study therefore has the potential to improve our understanding of the obstacles to conducting high-quality research with this very vulnerable population, and in the medium term, could help to improve the stability of foster placements and the emotional well-being of children in care.

The therapeutic imagination: using literature to deepen psychodynamic understanding and enhance empathy

Robert Fleming

Robert Fleming

London
UK

Robert Fleming   *Email: Robert.fleming@slam.nhs.uk

Jeremy Holmes has been straddling many domains for decades. He is a retired consultant psychiatrist and psychoanalytic psychotherapist who worked for many years in both the NHS and private practice. He is an academic and a practitioner, a skilled writer and commanding lecturer. His formidable output of over 200 publications has covered the ethics and the practical application of psychotherapy. However, perhaps his most important contribution has been in providing a clarity of perspective on the overlaps between attachment theory and psychoanalysis. In this book he revisits many of his essays written during his 35 years of work and presents his argument for the enhancement of the creativity of psychotherapists and thereby their patients through the therapeutic imagination.

The central thrust of the work is that there are many similarities between the literary and the psychotherapeutic imagination and therefore ‘literate therapists make better therapists’. Holmes is clear that rather than use psychoanalytic insights into art (and many have done this), he wants to bring ‘artistic insights to bear on clinical work’ (p. xii). His book is in four interlinked parts. Holmes begins by exploring the manner in which poetry and novels can develop the psychotherapist’s ‘imagination-in action’. He then approaches the overlap between psychotherapy and literature from an attachment theory perspective with particular emphasis on therapeutic change. The third section uses literature to focus on the specific areas of narcissism, anxiety, splitting and bereavement. The last section is a bold attempt to explore the sometimes difficult relationship between psychiatry and psychotherapy, again using literature to tease out the tensions. The art of psychotherapy and the science of psychiatry are juxtaposed.

Holmes traces the roots of the therapeutic imagination from German Romanticism via Coleridge and Bion. However, somewhat paradoxically, he argues ‘that imagination can be systematised and anatomised, and that it provides a useful framework for thinking about the components of psychoanalytic activity in the consulting room’ (p. 4). During my child psychotherapy training in the late 1980s, I recall Margot Waddell (1989) urging us to read George Eliot’s novel Daniel Deronda (1876) for a good example of transformation. It was a pleasure to come across Holmes using the same work in the key opening chapter. In a close analysis of the section in the novel when Deronda manages to intervene therapeutically as Mirah contemplates suicide by drowning, Holmes describes the similarities with the psychotherapeutic process using a five-stage model of the therapeutic imagination.

Nigel Carter and Jo Russell

Jo Russell

Jo Russell  

Two of our book reviews found at the end of this issue discuss works which raise questions, concerns, and thoughts about the essential value and current practice of psychoanalytic work in the contemporary workplace. Marcus Evans’ Making Room for Madness in Mental Health looks at the role of psychoanalytic thinking in responding to the needs of psychotic patients and argues that psychoanalysis enables services to identify the institutional defences which can be unconsciously activated by ‘psychotic communications’. Psychoanalysis, the NHS and Mental Health Work Today, edited by Alison Vaspe, is even more explicit in its identification of the need for psychoanalytic thinking to alleviate some of the pressures felt by those working within the present-day UK National Health Service.

These book reviews allude to a fundamental hypothesis that in order to better understand the external results of internal processes, be it in a single psychotic patient, or a mental health service department, the causative processes, which may well be unconscious and unclear to those directly involved, need to be identified and explored. The tendency and, as both books make clear, prevailing institutional culture, may actually be the opposite of this; to focus on the surface, the external and the conscious. These two books may well be informed primarily by reference to UK workplaces, yet it is surely not a UK-only matter, this ongoing battle to justify the place of psychoanalysis and child psychotherapy within mental health services and mental health culture. But how to do it? How to explain, inform and demonstrate the importance of psychoanalytic thinking and clinical practice? The five diverse articles in this issue, serve as an exemplar of the range of responses that child psychotherapy can contribute to the debate.

We lead with the updated critical review of the evidence base for psychodynamic psychotherapy for children and adolescents compiled by Nick Midgley, Sally O’Keeffe, Lorna French and Eilis Kennedy. Referring back to the earlier Midgley and Kennedy review of 2011 (Midgley and Kennedy, 2011), the authors bring us up to date by including research published in the intervening years and speak of ‘considerable developments’ in how our work with young people is being evaluated. The study reminds us of the findings of the previous report and shows how the evidence base has grown in the past five years not only in size, but also in the scope and variety of psychodynamic clinical work that is undertaken with children and young people. This research includes children with specific diagnoses, mixed diagnosis and results from Randomised Control Trials, as well as other research designs.

Editorial

Jo Russell

Jo Russell

Jo Russell  

Making a home in a new family is no small matter. The unconscious ease with which a content mother and her own lively two year old meld bodies and minds as she mediates his world to feed him or limit danger or to extend his horizons, may appear fluid and natural. But as all of us who have observed babies at close quarters know, such a beautiful relationship is hard won. It requires a carer sufficiently free of his or her own survival needs, one whose own psychological development has proceeded in a ‘good enough’ way, and intact healthy brains on both sides. The disposition of carer and infant and the match or ‘fit’ between these two will play a part. The inborn capacity of each to tolerate frustration will be important, and may influence their capacity to repair ‘ruptures’ in a felt sense of attunement. A legion moment-by-moment steps in their psycho-bio-social dance will have to accrue to construct the living dynamic of a secure base. Put in this way every well-attached child is not far short of a wonder. Fostered and adopted children, together with those who have had multiple family losses through violence and conflict, have so often not had the chance to achieve this, and certainly not at the very start when it mattered most. They do not arrive in new families with the happy freight of security, but instead with the vexed baggage of relational trauma.

And so in this special issue we are pleased to present seven papers which investigate and theorise precisely this matter of the struggle to make a home in a new family from multiple perspectives: the internal dynamics of finding or making a home, the powerful emotional effects of caring for emotionally ‘unhomed’ children, our therapeutic technique and our involvement and interventions as a professional group in the UK today. How can we best understand the complex internal landscapes of these unhomed children and how can we best help them become firmly settled within their new families?

Our title for this special issue aims to capture a central theme from all these papers but owes most perhaps to Simon Cregeen’s notion of finding ‘a place within the heart’. We lead with his paper which tackles the difficulties of children who arrive in new families bringing with them internal parental objects that are untrustworthy and abusive. Cregeen argues that the transformation of these to more benign objects requires the new parents to be able to make room internally for the projected parental objects of their adopted children and to receive these with non-judgemental curiosity in order to be able, in due course, to offer a new imagining of the original birth couple from which their children were born. His emphasis on the internal work which may need to be done by adoptive parents and which may need to be facilitated by a skilled psychotherapist is distinctive here, illustrated by his work with a couple who could only begin to fully embrace the children they had adopted once they had first re-worked established fears and defences regarding their own creative capacities.

Editorial

Kate Stratton and Jo Russell

Jo Russell

Jo Russell  

We have all been adolescents. We have all had to contend with bodies under the siege of inexorable physiological imperatives, whether these were welcome or resisted, and which delivered an adult morphology that we had little choice but to make our peace with. Neuroscience is rapidly teaching us that the changes within the brain are no less physical and no less seismic. If we used to think of adolescent transformation as a mostly linear affair, tadpoles to frogs – breaking out of the egg, gaining limbs, losing a tail – we must now understand that what occurs within the human brain during puberty is a much more complex process which has more in common with the metamorphosis of the caterpillar. A section through a pupating chrysalis reveals not order but apparent physiological chaos, in which all caterpillar (larval) body parts appear disintegrated and no butterfly (adult-imago) parts are revealed. It appears that during human adolescence ‘synaptic pruning’ and the forging of new neurological pathways may be of an analogous order and manifest radical physical alterations in how the brain functions. Perhaps we should not be surprised at the emotional and psychological maelstrom that may ensue, and even less surprised where there has also been a troubled start in life. There is of course a corresponding raft of external, social, changes going on for the adolescent too. Every settled productive adult has had to negotiate a change of role and expectations, take on new responsibilities, steer their own course, become autonomous, work out who they are attracted to and how to be sexually intimate. From a developmental perspective our work with adolescents might almost be understood as a kind of psychoanalytic midwifery: where a complex psychological ‘birth’ seems to be stuck or to be going awry, we may be called in to accompany, intervene, encourage in order to help the young adult be ‘born’, capable of independent, viable and sexual life.

So this issue on a special theme of adolescence opens with three papers which tackle the reality of sexual and erotic transference, and the handling of this, within the psychotherapies of adolescent patients. As each author remarks, the literature on the topic has historically been somewhat slender, and in such a context we make a significant addition with the publication of these articles. Emil Jackson’s is a substantial paper both theoretically and clinically, but its key distinctive feature is the willingness with which he examines his own part in the dynamics generated between himself and the two young women he is treating. Jackson seems to be repeatedly asking himself ‘And what I have done (or not done) here?’ including the difficult question of ‘How might my behaviour be interpreted as sexually provoking?’ Jackson is concerned that we learn to investigate sexuality within the consulting room in a direct yet safe way, and offers his own defensive ‘errors’ and his corrections of these by way of illustration. His paper encourages us to ‘handle the explosive material’ (after Freud) but also cautions us to be fully aware of our timing of interpretations in relation to how firmly the work is established, and to keep a weather eye on the effect of our comments – do they inflame or relieve, help or hinder?

Intersubjectively oriented, time-limited psychotherapy with children: how does the therapist evaluate the therapeutic process and what are the therapist’s tasks?

Marianne Haugvik and Svein Mossige

Svein Mossige

Lørenskog
Norway
Outpatient Clinic for Child and Adolescent Mental Health

Svein Mossige  

time-limited psychotherapy, intersubjectivity, therapeutic alliance, mentalization, short term psychotherapy

Based on the therapist’s evaluations of three therapies, this research aims to study the therapeutic process in intersubjectively oriented, time-limited psychotherapy with children. A primary objective is to further develop the therapy method. The study comprises therapies with children 6–11 years of age, who had experienced difficult family situations. Each child received 12 therapy sessions. The number of therapy sessions with children and parents was agreed upon beforehand, and the therapeutic objectives were approved by the parents. Each of the therapy processes were evaluated by the therapist by answering three questions and filling in three forms after each therapy session. The forms were: The Feeling Word Checklist; an alliance form for the child; and a process form. The therapeutic alliance and the behaviour of the therapist during the therapy sessions are discussed on the basis of the total material. The following main tasks for the child therapist emerged: structuring the therapy sessions; following the child’s initiatives; participating and cooperating with the child; exploring the child’s expressions; and understanding and regulating emotions.

This paper describes a developmental psychotherapy undertaken with a physically disabled latency boy, with a background of significant developmental deficits and multiple psychological trauma, diagnosed by CAMHS as being on the autistic spectrum. Using an assessment framework following Anna Freud’s conceptualisation of developmental lines, pathology as a deviation from the norm was formulated. Assessments using standard psychological tests were made at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end of his therapy, in order to study the changes in his personality development. Standard assessment findings were also used to portray the fragmentation of the boy’s psyche in a concrete fashion, in order to facilitate his re-integration.

What to do if the mind does not develop? A psychoanalytic study of pervasive developmental disorders

Louise Allnutt

Louise Allnutt

London
UK
Children, Young People and Families Service, Tavistock Centre

Louise Allnutt   *Email: LAllnutt@tavi-port.nhs.uk

This volume, compiled of a broad range of case studies, is a valuable reminder of the impact that psychoanalytic work can have on groups of children where there are deficits and disturbances in symbolic function, imagination and the desire for shared meaning. It joins the well-versed debate about what can or cannot be done by psychoanalytic work; a necessary debate and exploration for the unsettled clinician in 412 the face of a child or adolescent patient who is apparently reluctant to make use of her therapist. I think we are working in interesting times as our understanding of neurodevelopment continues to demonstrate the centrality of relationships, and this volume is a helpful recapitulation and elaboration of the ways in which child psychotherapy has grown technically to encourage and facilitate the growth of the mind and, more importantly, its capacities.

To begin with the introduction: this is a scene setting exercise as might be expected, but there is an underlying argumentative tone here that, in my view, is not entirely necessary. It is an all too familiar starting point and one which seems to haunt the relationship between psychoanalysis and autism. Statements such as, ‘People who attack this method often do not know it at all or know it only by hearsay …’ (p. 3) come across as somewhat defensive and made me wonder whether there might ever come a point at which we will be confident to describe the work we do without immediately feeling we must refer to the detrimental impact of the earlier mistakes such as Bettelheim’s popularisation of Kanner’s concept of the ‘refrigerator mother’ (Kanner, 1943). Or indeed might we see a time where we can drop the assumption that other professionals or parents are not interested in, or do not understand, the value of the psychoanalytic contribution? Drawing on my own professional experience of working as a psychoanalytic clinician in an NHS service for children with developmental disorders for several years, my current view is that our only way to develop positive working relationships and greater understanding is through mutual respect and non-competitive co-operative working. My impression of most of the clinical work presented in this volume is that it is taking place in private practice as is usually the case in Italy. This volume is therefore not a text that has grown out of multi-disciplinary practice or integrated working and this may account for why there is both a freedom in Bertolini’s deeply felt expression of the psychoanalytic frame, and at the same time a sense that he is working in isolation and to some degree ‘against the grain.’ However, as the title declares, this is a ‘psychoanalytic study,’ and, broadly speaking, it is worth the read.

Psychodynamic psychotherapy for children and adolescents: an updated narrative review of the evidence base

Nick Midgley , Sally O’Keeffe , Lorna French and Eilis Kennedy

Eilis Kennedy

London
UK

Eilis Kennedy  

child and adolescent psychotherapy, evidence-based practice, effectiveness, efficacy, outcome studies, psychodynamic psychotherapy

While the evidence base for psychodynamic therapy with adults is now quite substantial, there is still a lack of research evaluating the effectiveness of psychodynamic therapies with children and young people. Those studies that have been carried out are also not widely known in the field. To help address the second point, in 2011, we carried out a review of the evidence base for psychodynamic psychotherapy for children and adolescents, which identified 35 studies which together provided some preliminary evidence for this treatment for a range of childhood disorders. The present study is an updated review, focusing on research published between March 2011 and November 2016. During this period, 23 additional studies were published, of which 5 were reports on randomised controlled trials, 3 were quasi-experimental controlled studies and 15 were observational studies. Although most studies covered children with mixed diagnoses, there were a number of studies examining specific diagnostic groups, including children with depression, anxiety and disruptive disorders. whilst the quality of studies was mixed, some were well-designed and reported, and overall indicated promising findings. Nevertheless, further high-quality research is needed in order to better understand the effectiveness of psychodynamic psychotherapy across a range of different disorders, and to ensure that services can provide a range of evidence-based treatments for children and young people.

Background

Greta is 16. After a traumatic birth she spent the first few years of her life moving from one country to another with her parents, because of their jobs. Greta is an only child and because of complications around her birth her mother could not have other children. When she was five years old her mother became ill with cancer and the family moved to the UK. As mother went into remission father left her for another woman, and this had a very significant impact on Greta, who started to suffer with psychosomatic symptoms and was very anxious. Greta is a bright and talented student but since a young age she has been bullied and has found it difficult to manage her emotions. When she was 11 years old she went to a high achieving girls’ boarding school. She found it very difficult to be away from her parents, struggled to fit in with her peers and was bullied. Greta was referred to CAMHS when she was 14 because of severe depression and panic attacks. She self-harmed and had persistent thoughts about taking her own life by jumping from the window of her room at school. When I started to work with her, Greta had stopped attending school and was spending half of the week with her mother and the other half with her father, depending on their work commitments. All Greta seemed to want was to be with her mother in what she called ‘the bubble’, in an almost infantile state of symbiosis. Every sign of her mother’s separateness seemed to stir up in her intense feelings of rage, which she often directed against herself. She was in competition with her mother’s job and seemed to fall into a state of fragmentation when she experienced her mother as emotionally unavailable, while also clinging onto an idealised view of her mother. She was more ambivalent about her father, whom she wanted to please but whom she also blamed for all the difficult events of her childhood.

I offered Greta intensive psychotherapy and the session that follows took place one year and a half after the beginning of her therapy, just before a Christmas break. We had planned to reduce the frequency of her sessions to once weekly after Christmas, working towards an ending in the summer. There had been some important developments in Greta since the beginning of therapy and she had returned to school as a day student. She had stopped self-harming and was overall more able to engage with life and with her peers and more hopeful about the future. However, as we approached the end of our work, Greta felt anxious and some of the symptoms of the early phases of our work seemed to re-emerge.

Clinical commentary by Lucy Alexander, child and adolescent psychotherapist

Lucy Alexander

Lucy Alexander

London
UK

Lucy Alexander   *Email: lucykalexander@hotmail.com

This is a very moving and vividly written session with a 16-year-old girl just before a Christmas break and just before sessions are going to be reduced from three times a week to once weekly, moving towards finishing the therapy in the summer.

Knowing that an ending is in sight sets the context for us to expect to see a regressed patient. We also know from the background information about the family that separation might be experienced as particularly dangerous for this girl and for her parents. We are told that complications in Greta’s birth meant that her mother was unable to have more children and also that her mother became ill with cancer when Greta was five years old, around the time when she would have started primary school. We hear that once her mother went into remission, her father left her for another woman and that it was at this point that Greta started experiencing psychosomatic symptoms. We are told that Greta was sent away to boarding school aged 11, another key point of separation, and, with the onset of adolescence, became deeply depressed and suicidal.

The picture presented is of an emotionally deprived girl with separated parents who from the beginning of her life have found it difficult to come together as a parental couple to think about the needs of their only child. Unsurprisingly, Greta struggles with relationships both with her own mind and with others. We do not have any information about intergenerational patterns of trauma but we might hypothesise that the trauma of Greta’s birth was not fully attended to and that instead her parents retreated into their jobs, the other babies in their lives, leaving Greta before she was ready to be left. The therapist describes Greta at the beginning of therapy as wanting to be in ‘the bubble’ with her mother and comments on her rage at the slightest move to separate. The picture is of a retreat into a primitive state of being. We might hypothesise that as a baby Greta did not experience a facilitating environment that adapted to her needs (her mother could well have been depressed) and that any impingement was experienced as an annihilation rather than a source of frustration or opportunity for growth (Winnicott, 1956). In parallel to her mother’s illness, which facilitates a move back home from abroad, Greta’s illness, aged 14, as she faces the daunting adolescent tasks of individuation and separation, provides the opportunity for a reworking of early relationships. Encouragingly this time her parents seek and find help in the form of intensive psychotherapy.

This paper describes state of mind assessments as undertaken by child psychotherapists. It considers the similarities and differences with an assessment for an ongoing child psychotherapy treatment intervention and is described here as a ‘package’ that is offered to the family, child and young person and also the referring colleague. It is suggested that the consultative aspect has more weight in a state of mind assessment. The stages of the assessment are outlined and include the initial consultation with the referring colleague, a meeting with parents, three sessions with a child or young person and feeding back to parents with further consultation to the referring colleague. The meaning of the request at any particular time is explored and influences the stance and the approach to the assessment by the therapist. A summary of a case example illustrates the different stages outlined here. The thinking and approach described may be particularly useful to trainees and those starting out as child psychotherapists in child and adolescent mental health services.

[[RunningHead]]

Understanding the ‘blind spot’ when children move from foster care into adoption‡‡

Sophie Boswell and Lynne Cudmore

Lynne Cudmore

London
UK

Lynne Cudmore  

adoption, transition, foster carer, attachment, loss, organisational defence

Current social work practice in the UK dictates that when children move from foster care into adoption, the transition takes place within 7 and 14 days, and usually there is no contact between the child and their former carer for several months after the move, if at all. Very little attention or research has been aimed at understanding the rationale for these procedures, or their impact on the children. Joining forces with social work colleagues in a Looked After Children’s team, two child psychotherapists carried out a piece of qualitative research to look at these moves in more detail, and try to tease out how and why these key decisions are made. Analysing data from interviews with foster carers, adopters and social workers, the researchers found that the emotional experience of the child, particularly their experience of losing their foster carer, loses centre stage in people’s minds during this transition, leading to what is described as a ‘blind spot’ across the network. A significant reason for this emerged, in that the children tended to be very compliant both during and after the move and lacking in any obvious distress at losing their former carers, despite having previously been described as passionately attached to them. The research showed that adults across the network, all struggling with intense anxieties of their own, tended to interpret this as evidence that the children were ‘fine’ rather than questioning what might be going on at a deeper level. These research findings are explored in the light of a knowledge base accumulated from a working understanding of attachment and loss in early childhood, and of the psychoanalytical phenomena of individual and organisational defences against loss. Implications for future practice are suggested.

[[RunningHead]]

Some comments on ‘The experience of puberty’ by Shirley Hoxter

Jonathan Bradley

Jonathan Bradley

London
UK

Jonathan Bradley   *Email: jbradley@tavi-port.nhs.uk

The modest, rather outdated title of this paper does scant justice to its brilliance and clinical depth. I am pleased that it is being drawn to the attention of clinicians working today because, having spoken to a number of psychotherapists from different generations, I have the impression that it is not as widely read as it should be, despite having been selected for the well-known collection of key papers from the Journal of Child Psychotherapy (Barrows, 2004). One possible explanation for this might be that ‘puberty’ now mainly refers to a physical event, used within a context of sexual education. This is far removed from its meaning in the paper where it is understood as a unique experience, an ‘external expression of the unconscious anxieties and conflicts aroused by pubertal sexual development’ (13 [p. 96]).

According to Hoxter, the onset of puberty is also a call to war, waged between adults and adolescents as an externalisation of oedipal rivalry. Now the paper was published in 1964, and it is interesting to consider the context in which she was writing. Following the popularity of the teddy boys in the 1950s and violent race riots in 1958, the early 1960s saw the emergence of two conflicting subcultures: mods and rockers. It is now difficult to imagine how in May 1964 the population was drawn into a melodrama (as the paper suggests) surrounding these opposing adolescent gangs, yet it is likely that anyone reading Hoxter’s paper at the time would have been well aware of these disturbances. Mods wore stylised suits, rode elaborately decorated Italian scooters and ‘adopted’ The Who, whilst rockers wore leathers, rode powerful motorbikes (without protective headgear) and listened to Elvis Presley! It is striking that this was a conflict played out in public between two adolescent factions. One possible explanation for the fury generated within the adult population is that it was rendered impotent, forced to watch passively, and to clear up the damage created by what seemed like hordes sweeping all before them, seemingly indifferent to the trail of damage left behind. Matters came to a head over the holiday weekend in May when several thousand mods and rockers were involved in rolling clashes in the southern resort towns. The BBC On This Day archive for 18 May 1964 contains accounts of out-of-control mobs doing damage to each other and vandalising property, and then also paying the consequences in the form of fines and imprisonment.

‘Sleeping beauties’: succession problems of adolescence

Mary T. Brady

Mary T. Brady

San Francisco
CA
USA

Mary T. Brady   *Email: mbrady66@earthlink.net
adolescence, succession process, psychic retreat, Sleeping Beauty, fairy tale, beauty

The author explores the succession problems of adolescence. She uses the Brothers Grimm’s fairy tale Sleeping Beauty to consider various characters and narratives possible in the analytic field during the succession process. Use of the characters in a fairy tale allows an analyst to play with the different roles the patient unconsciously assigns her. The author conceives of the avoidance of adolescent turbulence as a common reaction to adolescence, but one that can also become entrenched, and result in a restriction of emotional growth. The paper explores the psychic isolation of adolescence and the splitting required to manage the conflicting desires of the phase. The persistent absence of passion, including in the analytic process, constitutes a psychic retreat from developmental turbulence. The analyst of such an adolescent may need to allow them to be ‘somnolent’ for some time, but may eventually need to wake them (metaphorically) or even pierce the somnolent, avoidant state. The author uses clinical vignettes of late adolescents to demonstrate such transitions, exploring her countertransference experience as well as the reaction of adults to the succession process of adolescence.

Gillian Sloan Donachy

Alexandria

Gillian Sloan Donachy   *Email: gillian.sloan@ggc.scot.nhs.uk
loss of the sense of self, emotional impact, internal world, foster care, abuse, neglect, reflective practice

This paper is an account of a piece of research which involved interviewing six foster carers who had ended a placement with a child under the age of five with an early experience of abuse and neglect. The paper describes one of the themes that emerged from the data analysis, the loss of the sense of self in the foster carers, and argues that the experience of attempting to provide care for these children led to internal shifts in the carers that reverberated throughout the network around the child. The paper suggests that knowing about the external reasons for placement breakdown is not enough without taking into account the impact on the internal world of the foster carers and the emotional impact of attempting to provide care for a child who has experienced abuse and neglect.

[[RunningHead]]

Too close for comfort: the challenges of engaging with sexuality in work with adolescents

Emil Jackson

Emil Jackson

London
UK
Adolescent & Young Adult Service

Emil Jackson   *Email: ejackson@tavi-port.nhs.uk
transference, countertransference, adolescent psychotherapy, erotic transference, sexual transference, adolescence

This paper explores some of the ways in which sexuality can intrude into the psychotherapeutic relationship and present both opportunities and risks to our work with adolescents. It highlights some of the complexities of this area of the clinical encounter, exploring the particular difficulties encountered by both patient and therapist when sexuality emerges in the transference and countertransference. While we are well aware of the centrality of sexual development during adolescence, far less has been written about the way in which sexuality and the erotic transference emerges and impacts on both patient and therapist. Given the profoundly unsettling nature of this area of work and its capacity to disrupt our thinking and psychic equilibrium, it is easy to underestimate how much we are drawn to avoid, negate and defend ourselves against registering such experiences. Through the discussion of clinical material with two adolescent patients, this paper explores some of these dynamics, addressing some of the technical dilemmas that frequently challenge us in this area of work. These include questions about whether and when it is therapeutically important and effective to take up and interpret the emergence of sexuality more directly in the transference and some of the risks to our patients when we ‘play safe’ and fail to do so. Most importantly, this paper aims to facilitate further thinking and discussion about an important but uncomfortable and easily neglected area of our work.

‘Her Majesty the Baby’: narcissistic states in babies and young children

Anne Hurley

Anne Hurley

London
UK

Anne Hurley   *Email: ahurley@tavi-port.nhs.uk
narcissistic states, narcissistic defences, ordinary narcissism, mother–baby interaction, self-sufficiency, separation and loss, frustration, abuse, neglect and deprivation

This article considers narcissistic states in babies and young children with some reference to the myth of Narcissus in Ovid’s Metamorphosis. The object-seeking character of babies from the beginning of life is elaborated in connection with selected research from mother–baby interaction. This forms the backdrop to a discussion of withdrawal into illusions of self-sufficiency and denial of dependence in adverse circumstances. Two clinical cases are discussed in some depth. One boy whose superiority, self-reliance and pseudo maturity is prompted by anxieties around separation as he approaches starting school is considered within the parameters of ordinary transient narcissism. The lengthy psychotherapy of another child, who developed entrenched narcissistic defences as a response to traumatic, abusive and neglectful experiences in early life, and who needed considerable help, is described in greater detail. Some links are made with difficulties associated with the emergence from narcissistic functioning and encountering the pain of separation and loss.

Author biographies

Sophie Boswell is a psychoanalytic psychotherapist working with children and adults. She qualified as a child psychotherapist at the Tavistock Centre in 2003, subsequently working and teaching in various settings including CAMHS community settings, children’s centres, schools and nurseries. For several years she worked in a CAMHS team within Westminster’s Looked After Children department. She was also a member of Westminster’s Adoption and Permanency Panel, and a member of the NICE panel, producing guidelines on the wellbeing of Looked-after Children and Young People (2010). Sophie is the author of Understanding Your Baby (2003), part of the Tavistock’s Understanding Your Child series. She currently works in private practice in London.

Eva Crasnow is a child and adolescent psychotherapist who trained at IPCAPA at the British Psychotherapy Foundation (BPF). She completed her doctorate on the topic of contact supervision with Looked After Children. In addition to teaching roles, Eva currently works at the Gender Identity Development Service at the Tavistock and Portman NHS Foundation Trust and at the Anna Freud National Centre for Children and Families.

Simon Cregeen is Head of Child and Adolescent Psychotherapy in Manchester and Salford CAMHS, Central Manchester NHS Foundation Trust, UK, and a clinical tutor on the Clinical Doctorate training at the Northern School of Child and Adolescent Psychotherapy, Leeds, UK. His main areas of clinical work are with Looked After children and their networks, adoptive families, and parental couples. He has had a number of papers published in this journal and elsewhere. Simon is a member of the STPP (IMPACT) Steering Group and a co-author of Short-term Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy for Adolescents with Depression: A Treatment Manual (2016, Karnac).

Lynne Cudmore originally trained as a social worker and worked in London before training in psychoanalytic psychotherapy and working for 26 years at the Tavistock Centre for Couple Relationships. Her research interests included the impact of infertility or a child’s death on the couple relationship. Lynne was the programme leader for the Professional Doctorate in Couple Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy. She then trained as a child psychotherapist at the Tavistock Clinic going on to work in the Infant and the Family Mental Health Teams there, and founding the service for teenage parents. For six years Lynne worked within the Looked After Children’s team CAMHS in Westminster Children’s Services, and then as consultant child psychotherapist in the Perinatal Mental Health Team at Chelsea and Westminster Hospital.

[[RunningHead]]

Research digest

Introduction

This is a mixed Research Digest offering, first, a selection of recent articles about goals and outcomes in child mental health generally, and second, a group of articles presenting outcomes in parent–infant psychotherapy, till now an under-researched therapy modality.

Goal setting in therapy is a commonly used outcome measure in most CAMHS and is regarded both as a useful clinical tool in its own right and a personalised outcome measure. The articles below detail attempts to discover potential relationships between personal goals and treatment outcome, or between personalised goals and standardised measures. It is interesting to note that goals characterised as ‘existential’, that is, to do with understanding, thinking about oneself, and the future, did not have any corresponding items in standardised measures, strengthening the argument for the value of personal goal setting in psychotherapy. Jacobs et al. (2017, below) conclude:

There may be areas not captured by standardised outcome measures that may be important for children and young people and which may only be currently captured in goal measurement. There is an indication that we may not be measuring what is important to children and young people.

Jacobs et al., 2017: 170

Other articles explore how to make sense of differences in parents’ and children’s goals, where goal setting is seen as one factor within the framework of shared decision-making (SDM), the use of which is associated with better outcomes (Edbrooke-Childs et al., 2016), and parents’ goals in child and infant psychotherapy (Kenny et al., 2017; Odhammar and Carlberg, 2015), as well as parents’ own outcome in mother–infant psychotherapy (Salomonsson, 2017). The second half of studies in this Research Digest focus on outcomes for infants, mothers, and the effect of intervention on parent–infant interaction, in parent–infant psychotherapy. We list a few RCTs and meta-analyses of parent–infant psychotherapy (for example, Fonagy et al., 2017; Barlow et al., 2017, Salomonsson et al., 2017, and Goodman et al., 2015). Some studies found improved outcomes in measures of maternal mental health and parenting stress, others in the domain of parent–infant relationships and maternal sensitivity, while results for infant development were much less ascertainable. Most studies found no significant differences when one treatment was compared with another, and more data is called for. Finally, we have included an interesting re-reading of Klein’s own infant observation in the light of modern research in infant development (Aguayo and Salomonsson, 2017).

Putting down roots: the significance of technical adaptations in the therapeutic process with fostered and adopted children‡‡

Monica Lanyado

Monica Lanyado

London
UK

Monica Lanyado   *Email: monica@lanyado.com
developmental therapy, kindness, playing, moments of meeting, therapeutic transitional objects, technique and practice

Severely neglected and traumatised children have also suffered from a lack of the parental nurturing which is needed for ordinary emotional development to take place. Often their past experiences make them unable to utilise the nurturing that foster and adoptive families try to give them and they are delayed or stuck in their development. In therapy, when the early small signs of new emotional development start to emerge, they may be heralded by technical challenges to the therapist. Two examples are given in this paper, which are discussed in the context of Stern et al.’s ideas about moments of meeting, Winnicott’s concepts about transitional phenomena and playing, and Hurry and her colleagues’ thoughts about the therapist as a developmental object. It is argued that it is important for the therapist to be alert to the possible significance of these technical adaptations in terms of the child’s capacity for new emotional development. These often indicate that a watershed in the treatment has been reached and if positively responded to, that the patient is in the process of ‘putting down roots’ in the ground of the therapeutic relationship and starting to grow across a spectrum of developmental pathways.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Home, homelessness and nowhere-ness in early infancy

Joshua Durban

Joshua Durban

Tel Aviv
Israel

Joshua Durban   *Email: j-durban@inter.net.il
homeless, nowhere-ness, anxieties-of-being, autistic spectrum disorder, refugees

The construction of a sense of home in early infancy is a complex achievement. It is intertwined throughout life with the child’s pursuit of a safe physio-mental coverage. This process will be described as an interaction between: (a) a safe dwelling in the body-as-mother (constitution); (b) the internalisation of the mother-as-me (internal object space) and (c) establishing Oedipal triangular space which is responsible for the capacity to move between narcissism-as-a-home and the world-as-a-home. The construction of a home as an interplay between these elements is accompanied by distinct anxieties and unconscious phantasies. Disruptions in this early process, due to deficit, internal object relations or environmental factors, might lead to severe pathologies, mindlessness, hatred, violence and murderousness. A distinction will be made between these mental states of being-at-home, homelessness and nowhere-ness based on the corresponding levels of early development and typical anxieties. Home and homelessness are seen as more developed states of object relating accompanied by some capacity for feelings of loss, mourning and longing. Nowhere-ness, however, stems from early states of anxieties-of-being which are characterised by confusion between self and object, by nameless grief, nameless dread and devastation. The varieties of home, homelessness and nowhere-ness will be discussed with the help of clinical material taken from an analysis of a refugee child on the autistic spectrum and of his father. The role of psychoanalysis and of the psychoanalyst in promoting the creation of an internal home will be described with reference to technique.

Within or without: negotiating psychic space with an adolescent at risk of developing a narcissistic personality structure

Ian Paton

Ian Paton

London
UK

Ian Paton   *Email: ianpatonpsychotherapy@gmail.com
adolescence, destructive narcissism, sexualised transference, homosexuality, Oedipal triangle, separation-individuation

This paper examines a 22-month once weekly psychotherapy with an adolescent young man. My patient was one of a group of adolescents who, due in part to excessive aggression, envy, anxiety or confusion, has chronically evaded the intimate and dependent psychic contact with others that is necessary for psychological development. In my view, this comes about through a combination of external factors and internal predisposition, with the quality of care received during infancy playing a crucial role. These adolescents appear to be developing narcissistic modes of being in the world which if allowed to persist into adulthood would be seen as deeply entrenched clinical psychopathology. Managing separation and loss is one of the central aspects of adolescence, but these young people tend to intrude or merge with others with such aggressive force that recognising difference between self and other becomes difficult. In psychotherapy, this often takes the form of the patient’s inability to tolerate experiencing the therapist as a separate person, and when knowledge of the therapist as separate impinges on their view, they frequently react in a variety of primitively destructive ways. This paper seeks to explore these central ideas through a detailed examination of psychotherapy with a young man in whom such struggles predominate.

Working with and ‘seeing through’ the sexual transference in the psychotherapy of an adolescent boy

Fanny Elisa Lena

Fanny Elisa Lena

London
UK
Tavistock & Portman NHS Foundation Trust

Fanny Elisa Lena   *Email: flena@tavi-port.nhs.uk
sexual transference, adolescent sexuality, narcissism, containment, gaze

This paper explores the challenges and developmental opportunities of working with the sexual transference in psychotherapy with adolescents. Psychoanalytic contributions investigating the nature of adolescent sexuality and the developmental move from a narcissistic organisation to a capacity to form intimate relationships are reviewed, and the question of what happens when there is a lack of containment in infancy is addressed. The way in which unintegrated sexual impulses and phantasies can invade the therapeutic relationship is further discussed through the account of the weekly psychotherapy of a 16-year-old boy who formed a powerful sexual transference to his female therapist. The paper highlights how working through the sexual transference enabled this young man to face his developmental paralysis and begin to use the therapy as an opportunity for psychic growth.

[[RunningHead]]

The experience of puberty**

Shirley Hoxter

Shirley Hoxter

Shirley Hoxter  

Introduction

The specific feature which differentiates the adolescent from people of other ages is the experience of puberty, and much of the adolescent’s behaviour in the community may be seen as an external expression of the unconscious anxieties and conflicts aroused by pubertal sexual development. It also appears that some of the community’s reactions to adolescents express the anxiety of the adult when faced with the fact that a new generation is attaining sexual maturity. An adolescent girl reflected a wide-spread attitude when saying “I know what juvenile delinquency means, but I am not sure which word means ‘young person’ and which word means ‘criminal’”. The constant stories of teenage violence and teenage sexuality and the reactions of outraged protest, force upon one the realisation that prominent sections of the adolescent population and of the adult population alike are engaged in the warlike activity of acting out their oedipal rivalry.

This is often conducted in conformity to stereotyped patterns of conflict which enable both parties to avoid experiencing guilt and personal responsibility for the intense feelings of hostility and envy arising from their mutual sexual rivalry. Sometimes the conflict occurs on a vast scale and most of the population is drawn into participating in the melodrama at least vicariously. Or it may initially be conducted as a one-man war. A boy telephoned me late one might saying “I have urgent news to tell you. I am at war with the L.C.C.” This was followed by tenacious and partially successful efforts to get myself and other members of the Clinic staff to act in conjunction with him and to become involved in conflict with many County Council officials. It was only just possible to prevent him from extending his war to the police and to Interpol.

The physical maturation of the adolescent, with its greatly increased sexual drives, is simultaneously accompanied by a resurgence of the imperious feelings and phantasies which previously characterised the object relations of early childhood. The adolescent is faced with the task of relinquishing his parents as his original sexual objects and turning to others outside the family. This leads to further difficulties when impulses stemming from the infantile aspects of his sexuality continue to dominate his behaviour, both with his peers and with adults. The adolescent has the physical capability to put into action much which would appear mainly as phantasy in the young child. He can really attack, destroy, rob, murder or commit suicide and he can really have sexual experiences of a heterosexual, homosexual or perverse nature. [[RunningHead]]

The body in adolescence: psychic isolation and physical symptoms

Riccardo Lombardi

Riccardo Lombardi

Roma
Italy

Riccardo Lombardi   *Email: dr.riccardolombardi@libero.it

Mary Brady’s latest book is an exploration of adolescence, focusing in particular on body-related symptoms, such as cutting, anorexia, substance abuse, bulimia and even suicide, the extreme act of killing one’s own body. It is a highly relevant approach, not only because Brady considers thinking about symptoms and their resolutions as a fundamental aspect of psychoanalysis, but also because she explores the intricate relationship between mind and body, which is crucial for the development of our field. The title’s subheading underlines Brady’s tendency to relate physical symptoms to psychic isolation, a state which she sees as caused by difficulties with separation and the process of mourning for the adolescent’s parental figures at this extremely delicate time. In the book the idea of isolation has also, at times, a different and more profound meaning, namely the internal isolation from one’s self and body. The adolescent, Brady writes, faces a body that is ‘something apart and separate from the self’ (p. 12). Unfortunately the dissociation/integration of the body (see Lombardi, 2017) is not clearly addressed in this volume on adolescence, which is quite striking considering that one of the aims of the book is to focus on the body from a psychoanalytic perspective.

The book is divided into seven chapters, all rich in clinical material, which enables the reader to fully comprehend the dynamics being discussed. The first chapter ‘Unjoined persons’ addresses the isolation of the adolescent caused by separation from the parents, focusing in particular on different transitional moments, like the risky transition into high school and college. Brady highlights the fundamental importance of the adolescent capacity ‘to imagine her way into a new world’ (p. 18) through the imagination of a well functioning external couple.

The body seems to have a central role for Catherine, who focuses on clothes and shoes. Brady writes that she ‘seemed to be using her identification with me (trying on my shoes) as a progressive step in exploring identifications’ (p. 20). In my opinion, trying on new shoes and new clothes could also be interpreted differently as an expression of the attempt through the body to make sense of the experience of being an adolescent with a real body that is changing and moving towards adult forms and dimensions. In this scenario the analyst is not the primary object that needs to be introjected, but only an external catalyst, because the body is the mind’s primary object (Lombardi, 2002).

Reading Klein

Eva Crasnow

Eva Crasnow

London
UK

Eva Crasnow   *Email: ecrasnow@tavi-port.nhs.uk

Reading Klein is the latest publication from the New Library of Psychoanalysis Teaching Series (series editor Alessandra Lemma). Written by Margaret and Michael Rustin, it adds Melanie Klein to the other figures and groups in the series: Sigmund Freud, Anna Freud, Donald Winnicott, Hanna Segal, French Psychoanalysis, Italian Psychoanalysis together with volumes on technique and observation.

291

The aim of the series is to offer an overview of key subjects and theorists for those either studying or just interested in psychoanalysis. My first encounter with the series was in 2006 when I was at The Anna Freud Centre/UCL studying for the Psychoanalytic Developmental Psychology MSc. Reading Freud, written by Jean Michel Quinodoz (2005), provided me with a reassuring sense of authority – here was a ‘textbook’ that would provide some of the elusive answers that seemed so slippery and provoked such a range of opinions and responses among those of us encountering Freud for almost the first time. I returned to this ‘textbook’ when teaching seminars about Freud on the IPCAPA child psychotherapy doctoral training, perhaps seeking a form of validation when coming back to my training home as a now qualified graduate of the programme. On re-reading I was a bit surprised; the authority I had placed in the wished for ‘textbook’ had shifted and I found myself having alternative opinions and ideas about some of the concepts and the implications of these. It seems that in the nine years between readings, I had shifted enough to allow there to be multiple axes of authority and (hopefully) some increased flexibility of thought.

My hope for Reading Klein was to gain a better understanding of the development of Klein’s thought over time. I was mindful of Kleinian concepts, but knew little about Klein’s personal history or how, when and where her contributions to psychoanalysis emerged. The volume opens with the writers stating their aim: to present Klein’s ideas through her major writings, and their own accompanying commentary. There would also be attention given to where her ideas have led others, clinically and socially. My hopes it seemed, were to be met.

Making room for madness in mental health. The psychoanalytic understanding of psychotic communication

Robert Fleming

Robert Fleming

London
UK

Robert Fleming   *Email: Robert.fleming@slam.nhs.uk

This book is about the treatment of severely mentally ill patients and the supervision of the clinicians involved in this work. It focuses on adults but every child and adolescent psychotherapist I know has worked with this group in a direct or indirect way at some point as many of the parents or family members of children or adolescents in treatment have mental health problems. It should be essential reading for any psychotherapist wanting to understand more fully the potential contribution of psychoanalysis to all areas of mental health and it is perhaps especially useful in understanding the medical model (both strengths and weaknesses). Marcus Evans is well placed to explore this area having a background in psychiatric nursing before becoming a leading consultant psychoanalytic psychotherapist. Throughout the book Evans acknowledges his debt to many of the psychoanalytically oriented psychiatrists he encountered in his professional development.

The author sets himself an enormous challenge when he says he wants to ‘demonstrate the importance of the relationship between psychiatry and psychoanalytic psychotherapy in the treatment and care of patients’ (p. 203). Despite the contributions of leading psychoanalytic thinkers to psychosis over the last hundred years, the current hegemony in mental health services in the UK is arguably not amenable to the psychoanalytic model. The rise of manualised, time-limited and cost-oriented services have led to a shrinking of the space for thinking and a tendency to be blind to the psychological impact of this work on front-line staff. Evans makes a brave attempt to elucidate the potential for the relationship between psychiatry and psychoanalysis, stating, ‘… psychiatry needs psychoanalytic psychotherapy and psychoanalytic psychotherapy needs psychiatry’ (p. 203). I am tempted to say that he might have strayed into over-hopeful optimism that does not fit with my own professional experience.

It is important to state at the outset that Evans uses a definition of psychosis that is more than psychiatric symptoms. He describes it in terms of a withdrawal from reality and can thereby argue that it underpins apparently neurotic conditions and can therefore impact us all. This emphasis is indicated in the second part of the book title, ‘The psychoanalytic understanding of psychotic communications’. O’Shaughnessy writes in her foreword that Evans has shown that, ‘the psychoanalytic method does not keep insanity out of view, but rather tries to offer madness a habitat and human understanding’ (p. xxiii).

How to grow up or (nearly) die trying: developing trust in one’s own capacity for growth

Alexandra de Rementeria

Alexandra de Rementeria

London
UK

Alexandra de Rementeria   *Email: alexandra_de_rementeria@hotmail.com
adolescence, Oedipal humiliation, narcissism, grievance, mourning, intensive psychotherapy, suicidality

This paper is a single case study describing intensive psychoanalytic psychotherapy with an adolescent girl, an apparently bright and capable girl who was struck down at 15 by a double blow of trauma and loss. She cracked along her fault lines which, it is argued, were created during the ordeal of her psychic birth in the first year of life. It is proposed that ordinary Oedipal humiliations precipitated anxiety about dependency. While any adolescent is likely to have to grapple with these difficulties, the terrible life events that befell this girl compounded her dependency just when she might have been moving towards independence. In addition, the ordinary task of mourning childhood and familiar family relationships was obscured by the new and devastating losses that needed to be mourned. Unable to face this task, she spurned the support of her loving family and any potential good object and instead became dependent on manic over-achievement and grievance. The paper traces how the intricacies of the patient’s internal world slowly unfurled through the transference and countertransference and through her story as she told it to her therapist. The therapist describes the slow and difficult process of making links between that story and their experiences together in the consulting room. The theoretical concepts that enabled these links to be made are outlined and the ways in which they guided the therapist’s technique are discussed.
